To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) simple intransitive movements of the hands (flexion and rotation) can be distinguished in the contralateral primary motor cortex, (2) the distinction between the two movements is present at the level of the primary motor cortex and is not due to higher level motor areas, and (3) the difference in patterns of activity between the two movements does not reflect differences in amplitude of BOLD response, but rather differences in patterns of activity within the motor area.
simple intransitives can be distinguished in motor cortex.

simple intransitives can be decoded in primary motor cortex, but only when the decoding is done within the subject specific ROI that is defined functionally by the hand/wrist rotation and flexion movements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural representation of simple actions in the primary motor areas of the brain.
the neural representation of action.
the question of whether the motor system can distinguish between different actions in primary motor areas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the primary motor cortex is not only a motor area but also a cognitive area, and that it can be used to distinguish simple actions using multivoxel patterns.

the results of this paper show that the primary motor cortex contains a componential representation of simple actions, and that the componential representation of intransitive actions is not limited to the pre-motor cortex, as has been suggested previously.
the motor cortex encodes a variety of different movements, but not all movements are represented equally well.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MVPA is able to detect differences between movements that are not detectable by traditional methods.

the primary motor cortex is a 'componential' representation for action, with each component being represented by a distinct neural population, and that these components are organized by the effector and the type of movement, but are not organized by the direction of the movement.

MVPA is able to distinguish simple actions that are similar in their average BOLD contrast, and therefore are similar in their overall activation amplitude, and that this ability to distinguish simple actions is present in primary motor areas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MVPA over fMRI data may be a promising method to study the representation of simple actions in primary motor areas.
MVPA is a powerful tool to distinguish between different actions in motor cortex.
MVPA can be used to distinguish simple intransitive movements within the primary motor area.
